questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted the destination to be mainly English-speaking and wanted to go outside of Europe. I also wanted to take courses relevant for my area of studies, preferably courses not otherwise available at my home institution.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a really great experience, and I would highly recommend anyone considering going to go. I met so many nice and friendly people and got to experience a completely different way of attending university as well as a new culture.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Mostly it was easy to find. Sometimes you did, however, need to dig a bit on different websites to understand the system properly and get all the necessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive any specific assistance. The University did not arrange any meet-ups or social gatherings, but my fellow exchange students managed to arrange picnics and other get-togethers, which was a great way of meeting other newcomers.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
I received some information emails and an invitation to a party, but the latter very much appeared to be a scam, so I did not try to attend it.
There was a short presentation for exchange students, but it was pretty much the same information as in the emails, so it felt like a waste of time.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I lived at Tartu College, which was right next to the northern part of St. George campus. I lived with five other girls where we had our own bedrooms and a shared kitchen and bathrooms. The rent and location were great. Living there was nice most of the time, but our building was surrounded by construction sites, and we had mice on several floors for weeks before the administration did anything about it. I did, however, also hear about similar problems at other types of housing, so I think it might be hard to find something without pests or construction.
Tartu fills up really fast, and I already booked my room in April. It was nice living with other people.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Finding housing can be hard when you don't know the city and probably won't have the opportunity to visit apartments in-person. There are a lot of scams online, so definitely watch out for that.
It can be a good idea to start looking for housing early, but some places (e.g. Campus Coop) also only accept applications quite close to the start of the semester.
Living close to campus is great for staying social and feeling motivated to attend lectures, and public transportation can be a bit of a hassle at times. But I also met people that made it work just fine living a few kilometers away from campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of places had pests and/or construction either in- or outside. Finding a place with cheap rent was also hard, as a lot of students are in need of housing in the city. But it was also not impossible to find something decent.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My documents somehow went missing after I sent them, which caused a lot of stress, especially since I was not told what was wrong when I was contacted regarding insufficient documentation. It is hard to get into contact with the International Education, and even harder to ask them questions regarding registration. This was quite frustrating at times.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I sent my application, and later accepted an offer of admission. Gradually, I sent my documents and grades to the Mobility Online platform. I only got into contact with my host institution after they officially sent me a letter of acceptance, which was a few months before the semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I received powerpoints and documents with information.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. I got all the classes I wanted in the first round of applications.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to have your documents ready and checked well before they are needed.
Some classes are very hard to get into (e.g. computer science), while others are a lot easier to get a place in. Remember to have a backup plan and watch out for different deadlines.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took one 300 course and three 400 courses. I found that they were not that different in difficulty, but the 300 level course definitely felt more like a high school class during lectures, while the 400 level courses had lectures more like the ones at my home institution.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The workload varies a lot throughout the semester, and the final grades are based upon your work throughout the entire semester instead of just a final exam.
There were generally fewer lectures and rarely any tutorials. In general, we were not informed of which pages of the books to read for a given lecture, so you have to be able to figure that out yourself, as well as how to solve the assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: CHM338, CHM423, CHM455, CHM457

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really enjoyed the CHM338 course which had both a theoretical and practical part. Working in the lab was a lot different than at home, and we were able to do analyses and procedures otherwise not possible at UCPH.
CHM455 was also a great course where the focus was on current research and thinking outside the box based on the knowledge you already have. Very different from anything I've tried before, but also very inspiring!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The university has a mandatory health insurance that all students must pay for. It is not too expensive, and I heard it works just fine.
Most prices are indicated without taxes, and some places expect tips.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are generally really expensive, while eating out is often cheaper than in Denmark.
Otherwise the prices are quite similar.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
A very large variety of clubs were available, and those I attended were very friendly and open to new people. The two run clubs were my favorites!
There were several athletic centres with fitness areas, swimming pools, indoor and outdoor tracks, and different types of classes were available. Pretty much everything was included in the tuition price.
There were also frat parties close to campus, but I chose not to go as I heard a few bad rumours about them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Try out as many clubs and activities as you can! I met so many nice people and also got to talk to a lot of local students which can otherwise be hard as people are not very social at lectures and tutorials.
Definitely go for something you are interested in, but also try something you might not do at home.
Attend some of the varsity blues games, they are free for students and a great experience!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Niagara Falls, Scarborough Bluffs, the CN Tower, Toronto Islands, Distillery District, High Park, Algonquin Provincial Park, Bruce Peninsula National Park.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy. It took a few weeks for my English to fully catch up and understand some of the local phrases, but the culture is a mix of a ton of international cultures, so accents etc. are not unusual.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to social clubs and remember to exchange something like instagram tags to stay in touch! Most are pretty busy but also open to meeting up. I also studied with a lot of people at the library even though our courses were different. It was a nice way of spending a bit of time together without compromising our studies during exam season:)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None in particular. Usually when people say sorry a lot, you are expected to reply with "sorry", which I found confusing at first, but it is seen as being polite.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Everyone were really open and friendly. I was invited to Friendsgiving and birthdays by locals although we had only been talking a few times. Although the locals may not be super interested in talking about culture differences, I had some really nice conversations with them about everyday life and had lots of fun.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to keep track of important dates and deadlines.
Try to plan out a few trips/things you want to see before arriving - time flies once you get there!
Tough days will come, but talking to others (both people at home and new friends) can help a lot. It will get better:)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not underestimate the distances in the country. It may look small on a map, but even travelling from Toronto to Montréal takes at least five hours by train/car!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to experience life in a completely different culture and attending a university with a large campus filled with students and different opportunities was really great.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Missing people at home. I definitely underestimated how much the time difference affects calls and texts with people at home, and I missed out on several larger events which I was a bit sad about.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
